newsitem.title: UK: Air traffic to triple by 2017 says Airbus.
newsitem.headline: Air traffic to triple by 2017 says Airbus.

text.p: Airbus Industrie predicted on Thursday that the world's major airlines will need to buy 13,500 more aircraft worth $1.1 trillion over the next 20 years to meet a tripling in demand for air travel and to replace older aircraft.
The European planemaker said in the latest edition of its Global Market Forecast that demand for air travel would continue to grow at an average rate of 5.2 percent over the next two decades.
As a result, the world's 246 largest airlines were likely to need to acquire a total of 15,800 new and used airliners of which 2,300 aircraft were already on order.
Airbus reckoned that with just over 2,000 aircraft likely to be acquired from the secondhand market this left the manufacturers to do battle in an open market for another 11,500 new aircraft.
The firm said it expected demand for air travel would grow fastest in the next decade, at an average of 5.9 percent a year, slowing to 4.6 percent annually in the period 2007-2016.

It reckoned that growth in North America, already the busiest region in the world for air traffic, would average only 1.9 percent a year, whereas growth in Asia-Pacific markets would average over seven percent.

Air travel in China is expected to multiply sixfold in the period, growing at nearly 10 percent a year, helping to make the Asia-Pacific region the world's biggest air travel market by 2017 with a predicted 32 percent of worlwide capacity as measured by aircraft seats, from 25 percent currently.
Airbus said Europe's share will also increase from 25 to 29 percent whereas the North American market would account for 28 percent of world capacity, against 39 percent now.

Arch rival Boeing Co issued its own market forecasts on Tuesday, which also predicted that it had a $1.1 trillion market to play for over the next 20 years, but predicted that the world's airlines would get 16,160 new jets for their money.
The differences highlighted the current dispute between the two manufacturers over whether they should invest billions of dollars developing new superjumbo aircraft.

Airbus, which says there is and wants to spend over $8 billion on a new A3XX 550-seat aircraft, said it expected that the average size of aircraft would grow from today's 179 seats to 235 and there would be demand for 1,440 aircraft "larger than anything flying today."
In contrast, Boeing said on Tuesday that its research indicated that the market for aircraft larger than 500 seats was only 480 aircraft over the next 20 years.

Boeing recently announced it was not going ahead with plans to build a stretch version of the 747-400, which at 425 seats in three-class configuration ranks as the world's largest passenger aircraft. Airbus says that by launching an A3XX it would also be able to break into Boeing's current monopoly on the market for long-range aircraft with capacity of more than some 350 seats.

Meanwhile, Boeing predicted that demand for air travel was likely to average a slower 4.9 percent rate of growth over the next 20 years, cut from 5.1 percent predicted a year ago due to a slowdown in the U.S. market and lower Asia-Pacific estimates.

The Airbus consortium comprises Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
